messages.subject: Introduction to Distance Sampling (fwd)
messages.body_plain:
Apologies for advertising books on this list!  Many of you will be
familiar with our book, 'Distance Sampling:  Estimating Abundance of
Biological Populations', published by Chapman and Hall in 1993.  Although
out-of-print with C&H, we have placed the book on our web pages
(http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distancebook/), and have printed extra
copies for those who wish to purchase it.  We still receive orders
for the book, so members of the list may be interested to have an update
on plans to replace it.

'Introduction to Distance Sampling', by Steve Buckland, David Anderson,
Ken Burnham, Jeff Laake, David Borchers and Len Thomas, is due to be
published in July (UK) /August (USA) of this year by Oxford University
Press.  It will cover most of the material of the 1993 book (though will
omit more advanced material).  It will also have several new sections, and
the chapter on study design and field methods has been substantially
reworked and expanded.  Details can be found at

http://www.oup.co.uk/isbn/0-19-850927-8 (paperback, UK site)
http://www.oup.co.uk/isbn/0-19-850649-X (hardback, UK site)
http://www.oup-usa.org/isbn/0198509278.html (paperback, US site)
http://www.oup-usa.org/isbn/019850649X.html (hardback, US site)

We are also working on a companion book, 'Advanced Distance Sampling',
which we hope will appear in 18 months or so.

Finally we are in the process of completing a book called 'Estimating
Animal Abundance: closed populations', by David Borchers, Steve
Buckland and Walter Zucchini, which will be published by Springer later
this year. It is intended to make the bewildering variety of abundance
estimation methods more accessible to the uninitiated and more coherent to
the cogniscenti. In it we emphasize the fundamental similarities of the
methods and draw out the common threads that underlie them. It covers all
commonly used methods for closed populations (including distance
sampling) from the simplest to the most advanced.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: CONFERENCE: ICODS, Registration Announcement
messages.body_plain:
-------------------------------------------------
               INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON DISTANCE SAMPLING
                    Estimating wildlife abundance for
                   Ecology, Management and Conservation

                         July 30 - August 3, 2001
                          St. Andrews, Scotland

                     http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/icods/
             -------------------------------------------------
                           Registration Announcement
             -------------------------------------------------

NOTE: The deadline for early registration is the 31st May, 2001. Any
registrations received after this date will be liable to a =9C50 late fe=
e.

Invitation
----------

We invite you to participate in the first International Conference on
Distance Sampling, to be held on July 30 - August 3, 2001 in St. Andrews=
,
Scotland.  This announcement contains outline information about the
conference and linked workshops.  Please visit our web site for more
details.

Objectives
----------

The aim of this conference is to bring together for the first time all
those interested in the estimation of wildlife abundance using distance =

sampling methods. Determining the density or abundance of wildlife
populations is a key component of population ecology, wildlife managemen=
t
and biological conservation. For many taxa, distance sampling methods su=
ch
as line transects, point transects (variable circular plots) and trappin=
g
webs are the most efficient approach.  These methods are now in very
widespread use by biologists, and there have been many recent developmen=
ts
in the underlying theory that increase the scope of the methods.  The ti=
me
is right for a major international gathering.

Our major objectives are to:

-Bring together practitioners from a wide range of disciplines and syste=
ms,
as well as statisticians involved in methodological development

-Present examples of new research and best practice through invited plen=
ary
talks

-Provide a forum for the exchange of ideas, techniques and methods throu=
gh
contributed talks, posters and informal discussion sessions

-Provide world-class training for those new to the subject, through link=
ed
workshops to be held before and after the conference

We hope that the conference will prove to be a major milestone in the
application of wildlife survey techniques, leading to increased
effectiveness
of field studies and stimulating many new areas of research.

Conference program
------------------

The conference will be a mix of plenary papers, giving state of the art
reviews of theory and practice, and contributed papers and posters.  In
addition, meeting rooms will be available for delegates to schedule and
attend informal discussion groups on topics of their choice.

The following leading experts in the field have agreed to give plenary
papers. (The preliminary topic of their paper is given in brackets.)

- Colin Bibby
  Birdlife International, Cambridge, UK
  (Estimation of bird abundance and its relevance to conservation.)

- David L. Borchers
  University of St Andrews, UK
  (Unified models for estimating wildlife abundance.)

- Stephen T. Buckland
  University of St Andrews, UK
  (Overview of research linked to the Distance4 project.)

- Kenneth P.  Burnham
  Colorado Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit, Colorado, USA
  (Large scale, long term monitoring.)

- Jeffrey L. Laake
  National Marine Mammal Lab, Seattle, USA
  (Distance sampling of Antarctic pack ice seals.)

- Bryan F.J. Manly
  Western EcoSystems Technology Inc., Cheyenne, Wyoming, USA
  (Simultaneous estimation of population size and habitat selection by
  distance sampling.)

- Kenneth H. Pollock
  North Carolina State University, USA
  (Combining capture recapture and distance sampling, or Comparisons of
  detectability estimation methods for circular plots on birds.)

- Fred L. Ramsey
  Oregon State University, USA
  (A general paradigm for all variable area survey procedures.)

- Tore Schweder
  Department of Economics, University of Oslo, Norway

In addition to the scientific program, we are planning field trips and a=

full social program.

Linked Workshops
----------------

The conference will be bracketed by two linked workshops. The aim of the=
se
workshops is to train participants in the latest methods for design and
analysis of distance sampling surveys, including line and point transect=
s.
The workshops are taught by leading researchers in the field, using
industry-standard software.

- Workshop 1: Introduction to Distance Sampling, July 25-27
An introductory workshop, focusing on "conventional" distance sampling
methods, including line and point transects where detection on the
trackline or point is certain.  The workshop will be a blend of theory a=
nd
practice and participants will learn how to use the program Distance.
Participants will gain a solid grounding in both survey design and metho=
ds
of analysis for distance sampling surveys.

- Workshop 2: Advanced Techniques and Recent Developments in Distance
  Sampling, August 6-8
A workshop designed for those who are already familiar with the basics, =

where we will teach advanced material such as automated survey design,
adaptive sampling, incorporating covariates into the detection function,=

methods for where g0<1, and spatial modeling of density.  Participants w=
ill
learn some of the more advanced features of Distance.  This workshop wil=
l
take place after the conference to give us a chance to discuss new work =

presented there.

For both workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data =

sets, and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their data.

The number of participants on both workshops is strictly limited and, ba=
sed
on preliminary registrations, we expect both workshops to be
oversubscribed. To avoid disappointment, we encourage you to register fo=
r
these as soon as possible.

Sponsors
--------

ICODS is supported by the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research
Council and the Biometrics Working Group of the Wildlife Society.

Further information
-------------------

More information about the conference, including the registration form,
is at the conference web site: http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/icods/

If you would like a printed copy of this information or have any
questions about the conference, please contact:

  Rhona Rodger
  Conference Organizer
  Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
  Mathematical Institute
  University of St. Andrews
  St. Andrews
  Scotland KY16 9SS

  Tel:+44 1334 463813
  Fax: +44 1334 463748
  Email: ic...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk

I am using distance to analyze transects to determine avian abundance =
(analyzed in clusters) in agricultural fields.  I have tried multiple =
truncations, groupings, and models and have come up with 'best' models for =
each treatment/time period.  I originally used the default 'sequential' =
for adjustment terms and 'estimate variance empirically' for variance.  =
Should I go back and try the 'forward' adjustment selection and bootstrap =
for variance?  I know Distance Sampling  (pg120) recommends evaluating the =
bootstrap on the final model, but is this always a superior method of =
estimating variance?  I have noticed, for the few that I have already =
tried, that the CV for bootstrap is higher than the CV for the analytical. =
 Is this normal?  Thanks for the help.

Sandy Cederbaum

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sandy,

> >I am using distance to analyze transects to determine avian abundance
> >(analyzed in clusters) in agricultural fields.  I have tried multiple
> >truncations, groupings, and models and have come up with 'best' models for
> >each treatment/time period.  I originally used the default 'sequential' for
> >adjustment terms and 'estimate variance empirically' for variance.  Should
> >I go back and try the 'forward' adjustment selection

If you have "good" distance data (ie wide shoulder, smooth decline in
detection function) then it is unlikely to make much, if any difference.  In
theory 'forward' adjustment selection is more flexible than sequential
selection of adjustment terms, as it tests all potential adjustment terms to
see which is "best" to add next.  In fact, I'm not sure why this isn't the
default in Distance! -- I guess because (a) it is computationally more
intensive and (b) generally, for "good" data, you won't want/need to fit
high-order adjustment terms.  Maybe one of the other distance sampling gurus
can shed some light on this?  Anyway, as I said, it shouldn't make much
difference.

> > and bootstrap for variance?  I know Distance Sampling  (pg120) recommends
> >valuating the bootstrap on the final model, but is this always a superior
> >method of estimating variance?  I have noticed, for the few that I have
> >already tried, that the CV for bootstrap is higher than the CV for the
> >analytical.  Is this normal?  Thanks for the help.

It is superior in that it makes fewer assumptions, and admits more real
sources of uncertainty.

For fewer assumptions: you don't use the analytic variance estimate of f(0),
so you are not relying on the assumption that observations are independant
(although this assumptions still plays a role in selection of adjustment
terms).  If you use the percentile-based confidence limits you are also not
making any assumption about the distribution of the density estimate (the
parametric confidence limits assume it is log-normally distributed).

For more uncertainty, you are including the uncertainty due to selecting
adjustment terms.  You can also put in more than one key function (Model
Definition | Detection Function | Models, + button) to include uncertainty
due to selecting which key function to use.  You will end up with wider
confidence limits, but they will more accurately reflect your true
uncertainty.  For more on model selection uncertainty, see:

Buckland, Burnham and Augustin.  1997. Model Selection: An Integral Part of
Inference.  Biometrics 53: 603-618.

and part of

Burnham and Anderson. 1998. Model Selection and Inference. Springer Verlag.

One time that bootstrapping is a bad idea is when you only have a small
number of points or lines to bootstrap.  Ideally you want at least 15-20
points or lines before you consider using bootstrapping -- otherwise your
results will likely be quite unreliable.  This also applies to using points
or lines to give an empirical estimate of encounter rate variance.

Hope this helps,

 - Len Thomas

Thank you for your responses to my plea for help.  Listed below are the =

in clusters) in agricultural fields.  I have tried multiple truncations, =
groupings, and models and have come up with 'best' models for each =
treatment/time period.  I originally used the default 'sequential' for =

I go back and try the 'forward' adjustment selection and bootstrap for =
variance?  I know Distance Sampling  (pg120) recommends evaluating the =
bootstrap on the final model, but is this always a superior method of =
estimating variance?  I have noticed, for the few that I have already =
tried, that the CV for bootstrap is higher than the CV for the analytical. =
 Is this normal?")

1.  I would not bother with forward selection.  It was originally put in =
the code for research sake.  Also, you didn't say what you did regarding =
truncation but don't use AIC to select between different truncation points =
because as the data differs so does the likelihood and it has nothing to =
do with the model.  What happens with the variance on a bootstrap depends =
on your data and sampling.  The traditional variance using the squared =
cv's of each component assumes independence between the various components =
(detection, encounter rate, and group size).  If these are not independent =
then the bootstrap variance can either go up or down but typically down =
because the covariance between n and f(0) is negative.  If f(0) goes up it =
is because animals are less
detectable and therefore n goes down.  This can happen when your are =
sampling different habitats but have not stratified.  Imagine what would =
happen if some lines were in grassland and others in forested areas.  =
Likewise, you can get a covariance between group size and the number of =
groups.  If you get some areas in which there are few larger groups and =
other areas in which there are more smaller groups then there is a =
negative covariance between n and E(S).  The other difference bt the =
bootstrap and the std variance is the latter is conditioned on the model =
which includes both the choice of key and adjustment functions and the =
number of adjustments.  If you bootstrapped and included multiple =
estimators then the bootstrap variance will incorporate model
selection uncertainty which will inflate the variance.  The bootstrap =
variance will be more relaible as long as you are not getting a lot of =
fitting errors during the bootstrapping.  This can occur occasionally if =
you include the hazard rate model.

Hope this helps

Jeff Laake
